What you’ll learn

Why “randomness” as a single idea collapses useful distinctions

How repetition reveals stable patterns inside uncertainty

Why probability distributions are descriptions of those patterns

The property-lens you’ll use to compare every distribution in the book

When people talk about 

randomness in everyday life, they usually mean something like this: anything can happen.

The phrase is vague, but it feels right. When outcomes surprise us (when our plans fail, or when effort does not produce the reward we expected) calling the situation “random” seems like an honest admission of ignorance. It names the loss of control we feel when the world does not cooperate with our expectations. It’s like lottery, or a coin toss: we don’t really know what will happen.

But there is a problem with this way of talking about randomness. It flattens too much. Like an iron smoothing out the wrinkles on a piece of clothes, it hides numerous imperfections that could be useful for understanding the world in more detail.

It groups together situations that behave very differently. It places waiting in a checkout line, applying for jobs, investing money, aging, and rolling dice under the same mental label. By doing so, it stops us asking more precise questions, and we start treating uncertainty as a single force acting everywhere in the same way.

In other words, this flattening has a cost.

When all randomness looks alike, our expectations about the world become distorted. We expect fairness where there is none, stability where there is volatility, improvement where there is reset, and safety where danger hides in extremes. When those expectations fail (as they will, inevitably), we reach for personal, moral, or mysterious explanations. We blame ourselves. We blame others. We invent stories about hidden causes. Sometimes we even conclude that the world itself is broken.

But, what is actually broken is how we understand randomness.

Pitfall: moralizing randomness

When expectations fail, we reach for moral explanations: someone deserves it, someone cheated, the world is broken. This reflex often comes from using the wrong model of uncertainty.

If you’ve read the introduction, you’re persuaded (I hope) that randomness is real, and that uncertainty is unavoidable in life. The aim of this chapter is to show you that randomness, uncertainty, and noise are not featureless phenomena. They are structured. Different uncertain situations push back on us in different ways. They reward different kinds of actions, punish different kinds of confidence, and tolerate different kinds of strategies.

There so much important detail in those wrinkles, and smoothing them out destroys valuable information.

Treating all randomness as the same erases those differences. It turns our judgment into mere guesswork. It also encourages persistence where restraint would be wiser, and caution where persistence would pay off. Very often we feel confident making some kinds of predictions and acting on them when not acting would be a much smarter choice. And equally often, we’re too timid to do something else because we feel the outcomes are too chaotic and unpredictable to even care.

This ‘flat’ approach to randomness also affects how we perceive our society and outcomes (both ours and others’) that occur in it. It makes some failures feel unfair and some successes feel deserved when neither conclusion is justified. We scoff at material inequality and see it as irreputable proof that our society is unjust; we perceive fame as well-deserved and react with shock when we discover that it could also hide a lack of talent.

Key idea

The task of critical thinking does not begin by eliminating randomness. That cannot be done. It begins by noticing that randomness itself comes in different shapes.

The main task of this book is to teach you more about those shapes. Once you start seeing them, you’ll be able to understand our world in a much deeper way. You’ll start to see the patterns below the surface.

It’s the closest thing you’ll ever get to ‘seeing the code’ that underlies our everyday reality.

Calling something random often sounds like the end of inquiry. If outcomes vary and surprises occur, what more is there to say?

Quite a lot, as it turns out.

Although individual outcomes remain unpredictable, uncertain situations tend to repeat. People wait in lines again and again. Messages arrive repeatedly. Attempts fail, succeed, or fail again. Over time, these repetitions leave traces. Patterns begin to appear, not at the level of single events, but at the level of many events taken together.

It’s important to stress a caveat here, so you’re not led into thinking that knowing about them will give you some supernatural insight: these patterns are not guarantees. They do not tell you what will happen next because they can’t. The only thing they can do is describe tendencies: what happens often, what happens rarely, and how outcomes are distributed across possibilities.

This is an important distinction. I want you to commit this to your memory.

Many people are confused about this because they can’t reconcile that both randomness and order can exist together in the same system, simultaneosly. Almost nothing is perfectly ordered or disordered; everything exists on a spectrum. Uncertainty at the level of individual outcomes can coexist with regularity at the level of patterns. The fact that you cannot predict exactly when the next email will arrive does not mean that emails arrive in a completely shapeless way. The fact that you cannot know which job application will succeed does not mean that success and failure scatter without structure.

They key here is to look at repetition. It will tell us how much order and disorder there is, and what ‘shape’ they take.

Some uncertain situations produce outcomes that cluster tightly; others spread them widely. Some generate many small deviations and few extremes; others hide their most important consequences in rare events. Some forget the past almost immediately; others accumulate the effects of small differences until they dominate everything else.

One might be tempted to ascribe these varied differences in displays of randomness to our psychological impressions, they ways our minds construct stories about reality. True, our psyche plays an important role in this process. All understanding is mediated by the structure of our minds.

But what we are talking about here are not properties of psychological impressions. They are properties of the processes themselves. There is something about our world, independent of how we perceive it, that forces randomness to behave in structured ways. Our job as critical thinkers is to understand these structures.

Seeing these regularities matters because human judgment is shaped by exposure. When we experience uncertainty repeatedly without recognizing its structure, we’ll make (sometimes costly) mistakes. We’ll ascribe meaning to a series of repeated events, we’ll think that some streaks indicate trends, and believe that rarity equals impossibility.

For example, after waiting longer than usual in one line, we assume it is “slow,” even though nothing about it has changed. If you’re a driver, you’ll understand this immediately: very often we change lanes because the one next to us seems much faster, only to remain stuck in traffic for pretty much the same time. Or, after receiving several rejections in a row, we conclude that something is wrong with us, even when the process itself resets each time. When a video suddenly goes viral, we search for hidden intention or genius, even though similar content often disappears unnoticed. When markets remain calm for a long time, we begin to treat extreme events as impossible rather than merely rare.

Recognizing regularity within randomness will not remove uncertainty. But, it will give it some contours.

And sometimes, even faint countours are enough for us to be able to reason and do things, even when the outcomes remain fundamentally unknown.

Key idea

Unpredictable outcomes can still produce stable patterns once you look at repeated instances.

To start seeing things differently, we have re-shape our perspective.

Human attention is naturally drawn to single outcomes.

We remember the interview that went badly, the message that never received a reply, the sudden success that seemed to come out of nowhere. These moments feel decisive because they are vivid. They are emotionally charged. They happen to us.

However, the problem is that single outcomes are almost always misleading.

A missed train feels like evidence of bad timing. A failed exam feels like a verdict on intelligence, and a lucky break feels like confirmation of talent. Yet none of these events, taken on their own, tell us much about the process that produced them. They are isolated snapshots taken from a moving system.

Instead of focusing on the snapshots, we have to look at the entire series.

So, what changes when we stop looking at one outcome and start looking at many?

We begin to see patterns.

Here are some examples. A single coin flip is uninformative, it doesn’t tell you much about the coin, or the next flip. But, flip it a hundred, or a thousand times, and you’ll see some balance. You might not know the result of the next flip, but you’ll know, roughly, the result of the next one hundred or a thousand. Similarly, one long wait in traffic on some street in some city is not always indicative of how congested the street is, yet many waits at the same spot will reveal congestion patterns.

When we widen the frame, meaning emerges.

This shift from individual events to collections of events is the conceptual move that good critical thinkers must make. That move necessitates introducing the idea of probability distributions.

The term may sound technical, but the idea is simple. A probability distribution is a way of describing how outcomes tend to appear when an uncertain situation repeats (how outcomes are distributed). It does not live in any single result, but in the pattern formed by many results taken together. It answers questions like: which outcomes are common, which are rare, and how widely they are spread.

Seen this way, a probability distribution is a description of structure within variability, rather than a mathematical object, even though many people learn about it as a mathematical object first. It captures the shape that randomness takes when we stop focusing on isolated events and start paying attention to how outcomes arrange themselves over time.

Definition: Probability distribution

Probability distribution is a shape that tells us how random outcomess appear when a situation is repeated many times.

An ensemble is simply a set of similar uncertain events viewed together. You do not need mathematics to understand this idea. You already use it intuitively. When you say that a restaurant is “usually crowded,” that a bus “often runs late,” or that a certain kind of content “rarely takes off,” you are reasoning at the level of ensembles, not individual cases.

Some outcomes appear frequently, others occasionally, others almost never. Some deviations cancel out over time, while others accumulate. None of this is visible when attention remains fixed on what happened this time.

This is why focusing too closely on individual outcomes distorts judgment, and why we need to think in terms of ensembles and distributions.

Probability distributions live at the level of ensembles. They do not tell us what will happen next. Instead, they tell us what kinds of outcomes belong to the same underlying process.

Note, however, that these ensembles can be either discrete or continuous. That is, they can be all identfied beforehand (like in a game of dice where each number on the face of the die is specified) or they can belong to a certain range that admits infinite parts. For example, human height is this kind of an example: if we focus on extreme precision, there are infinitely many heights people can grow to (within a certain range, from say 2 to 8 feet). Probability distributions are used to describe both kinds of ensembles.

Key idea

A probability distribution describes the pattern formed by many outcomes, not any single outcome.

To understand probability distributions accurately, you must be familiar with the concept of 

probability as well, and I trust you have at least a passing knowledge of it. As it happens, probability itself is not an easy concept to define and philosphers and mathematicians disagree about the most appropriate definition.

But, we don’t have to succumb to the temptation to disagreement. We can take a conciliatory and minimalistic approach an define it as simply 

an information about what can we expect from the outcome of some random process, expressed on a scale from 0 to 1. If we say that the probability of flipping heads with a fair coin is 0.5, we simply mean that we have 50% chances of seeing heads (or 1 in 2). The 0 to 1 scale maps to 0 to 100 in everyday parlance when we express it using percentages.

hierarchy.lvl2: Probability distributions as maps, not oracles
Probability distributions as maps, not oracles

records.content:
Once patterns of randomness become visible, a natural temptation is to treat them as forecasts. Many people, expert and laymen alike, feel the pull of this temptation.

If outcomes arrange themselves in regular ways, if some results appear often and others rarely, it is easy to slide from description into expectation. Structure begins to feel like foresight and orientation implicitly turns into prediction.

But, I’d like us to exercise caution here. This is where probability distributions are most often misused.

What a distribution provides is not a promise about what will occur, but a characterization of the situation itself. It tells you how outcomes tend to be arranged, how widely they spread, and where surprises are likely to appear. It distinguishes between environments where deviations are mild and those where rare events dominate consequences.

This distinction matters because knowing the terrain is not the same as knowing the path. You are not a Gandalf.

A probability distribution is like a map. A map does not decide your route. It shows what routes exist, how they connect, and where the dangers lie. Using a map well does not guarantee success, but it prevents certain kinds of mistakes, like walking off a cliff, mistaking a detour for progress, or assuming all roads are equally safe.

Probability distributions are maps for reasoning under uncertainty.

They limit our interpretation to what is possible, showing us explicitly what can happen and what cannot. They also discipline our explanations, keeping our focus on what are most and least likely outcomes. They also prevent us from demanding precision where only tendencies are available, warning us that we must be humble when faced with randomness. If you’re frustrated when you follow probability distributions, it’s likely because you treated them as guarantees rather than guides.

Simply put, pobability distributions shape how we interpret what we see. They limit the kinds of explanations that make sense and prevent us from exaggerating things or coming up with wildly implausible explanations. They also remind us that some situations only support rough expectations, not precise conclusions.

By doing so, probability distributions give boundaries to uncertainty. Within those boundaries, our judgment still matters, because decisions still involve risk and outcomes still vary. But without some guides, our judgment will miss it’s mark. So, what they give us is orientation: a clearer sense of what kinds of expectations are justified, and which reactions are out of proportion to the situation at hand.

Pitfall: Not an oracle

Probability distributions are rough guides to reasoning under uncertainty, not magical guides for predicting the future.

Up to this point, we have talked about randomness, regularities, ensembles, and patterns. All of that groundwork leads to a single practical question:

How, exactly, do uncertain situations differ from one another?

If probability distributions were just labels for different kinds of randomness, they would not be very useful. Their real value lies in the fact that each one captures a distinct way uncertainty behaves, and that behavior can be described systematically.

Every probability distribution answers the same small set of questions.

These questions are not mathematical or technical, though they can be (and often are) described using mathematical formulas. Statisics excels at making them as precise as possible. But, here we will talk about them as questions we already ask implicitly when we act in any uncertain situation in life. As you will see, they are intuitive and practical.

What probability distributions do is force those questions out into the open.

You can understand these questions as properties (or features) every uncertain situation will have. While they all differ from one another, there is a structure they all share.

Below is the conceptual lens this book will use throughout. Every distribution you encounter later will be described using the same set of properties. This will allow us to compare different uncertainties, transfer concepts from one to the other, and ultimately make good judgments.

Question: Is there a meaningful sense of what “usually happens”?

Some uncertain situations have a stable center. Most outcomes fall near it, and deviations tend to correct themselves. In other situations, the idea of a “typical case” is misleading or even meaningless.

This determines whether averages inform judgment, or distort it.

Question: How important are rare outcomes?

In some environments, extreme events are negligible; they exist, but they do not dominate consequences. In others, rare events matter more than everything else combined.

This property tells us whether ignoring extremes is harmless or dangerous.

Question: Does the process remember the past?

In some situations, each attempt starts fresh. Past failures do not improve or worsen future chances. In others, history matters. What happened before can change what can happen next.

This is important because it can help us understand situations in which continuing with some actions might be futile, and to distinguish with those in which it shouldn’t.

Question: Do small differences wash out, or do they compound?

Some uncertain processes are self-correcting, in the sense that early deviations from what’s expected fade, and the process returns to normal. Other processes amplify differences over time, and tiny advantages grow into lasting divergence.

This property explains why some inequalities stabilize while others explode.

Question: How far ahead can reasoning remain useful?

In some environments, short-term reasoning works but long-term prediction collapses. In others, even rough long-range expectations retain meaning.

This tells us how detailed planning should be, and helps us recognize when our plans become overtaken by too much (unjustified) confidence.

Question: What kinds of behavior make sense here?

Every uncertainty rewards some strategies and punishes others. Persistence, diversification, caution, aggression, patience, all of these can be rational or foolish depending on the shape of the situation.

That’s why knowing more about probability distributions and their properties can be used to transform unerstanding into agency: a concrete idea and a plan for action in the world determined by uncertainty.

In a fundamental way, these questions, and the properties they reveal are the interface between uncertainty and action.

When people feel that the world is unfair, unpredictable, or hostile, it is often because they are applying the wrong expectations to the wrong kind of uncertainty. They expect memory where there is none; typicality where there is none; safety where extremes dominate.

Probability distributions give us a disciplined way to avoid those errors.

How to read the chapters that follow

records.content:
From this point on, the structure of the book will be deliberate and slightly repetitive.

That repetition is not accidental. I want you to understand the shared structure and learn how to see below the surface of reality.

Each of the following chapters examines one recurring shape of uncertainty. You will encounter that shape first through an ordinary situation: something familiar enough that you can recognize yourself in it. Only after that intuitive grounding we’ll describe it using statistical and scientific terminology. The aim is not to make you versed in professional jargon, but smart enough to make personal judgments in your life, every day.

As you read each chapter, resist the urge to treat it as a self-contained topic. The value of these chapters lies in comparison.

Every chapter asks the same set of questions:

Is there a meaningful sense of what usually happens?

How important are rare outcomes?

Does the past matter?

Do small differences accumulate or disappear?

How far ahead can reasoning remain useful?

What kinds of action make sense here?

You will not always see these questions labeled explicitly. Often they will be answered indirectly, through examples, contrasts, and consequences. Your task as a reader is to notice how the answers differ from chapter to chapter.

Do not aim to memorize definitions. Instead, try to recognize patterns. When you encounter a situation in your own life (a delay, a streak of failures, an unexpected success, a sudden shock) the most useful question to ask is: what kind of uncertainty is this?

Some chapters will feel immediately intuitive. Others may resist understanding at first. But, no matter how much you are (un)familiar with the topic we’ll cover, learning about probabiity distributions will change your outlook on life. Trust me on this. I’ve seen that change in myself as well.

Finally, pay attention to the exercises.

They are not there to test your memory. They are there to force a mind habit: to recognize which shape of randomness you are dealing with, which expectations are justified, and which actions make sense given the kind of uncertainty involved.

I do not promise any certainty in this book. I offer some orientation.

And orientation is often enough to act without fooling yourself.                            ...

Exercise

Pick three situations from your life where you acted without knowing the outcome.

For each situation, answer:

Describe the situation (3 lines). What was uncertain? What action was required?

Describe the properties of the situation (short answers).

Typicality

Extremeness

Memory

Accumulation

Predictive Horizon

Expectation vs outcome (2–4 lines). Where did your expectations fit the situation? Where did they clash?

Action audit (bullets).

Was persistence rational?

Was caution rational?

What would you do differently now?

One-sentence reflection: Which mistake were you closest to making: misreading typicality, ignoring extremes, expecting memory, or assuming accumulation?

Perhaps I don’t have to tell you that uncertainty is a fundamental aspect of our lives. From the moment you wake up in the morning and gather your first thoughts, to the moment you drift away in sleep, cushioned in your comfy bed, you’re engulfed in the world without any guarantees.

You don’t know if you’ll wake up the next day. If you lucky and you do, you have no idea what will happen. Will you be happy, experience joy and success, or will your existence be marred by misery and misfortune? Will you achieve your goals? Will your actions yield results?

None of that can be known to us. That’s simply the nature of the world we live in.

Uncertainty is not a glitch in an otherwise perfectly smooth reality. It’s also not a temporary problem caused by missing information. It is a structural feature of reality. It’s inescapable. Nothing we try to do leads to any definite and certain outcome. Get out of the house and try to catch a train: sometimes you will catch it, sometimes you won’t. Sometimes you’ll wait 5 minutes, sometimes half an hour. Nothing is perfetly certain, even in the proverbially precise Switzerland.

While we’re at the mercy of this whimsical lord every moment of our waking lives, it doesn’t mean we are completely powerless. Fortunately, there are ways to reduce our uncertainty and at least have some idea about what might happen next, so our actions are not completely in the dark.

Those ways are the main topic of this book.

The path towards reducing uncertainty leads through the understanding of patterns the randomness of our daily experiences manifests itself. These patterns (we will call them shapes) are everywhere and the aim of this book is to help you recognize them, understand their nature and prepare strategies to ensure that when you do things in life (from crossing the street to choosing a career), you know what you should and shouldn’t expect.

The term professionals (scientists, statisticians, researchers, and philosophers) use for these ‘shapes’ is 

probability distributions. This piece of jargon hides an amazingly complex, yet extremely useful lesson about the reality we share: there is not a single uncertainty out there, but many of them (thus it would be more appropriate to call them ‘uncertainties’, using a plural rather than a singular).

Once you learn to recognize the shape of the uncertainty you are facing, many familiar confusions dissolve. You will be able to act in uncertain situations with a much greater understanding of what are you doing. You’ll be able to predict the most likely outcomes with greater confidence. And, you’ll also learn to distinguish situations worth the risk from those that aren’t.

Probability distribution is a staple concept in science. There is not a single scientist in the world worth the name who is not aware of it’s meaning and purpose. Understanding probability distributions helps scientists conduct experiments, derive conclusions from them, and make distinctions between mere accidents and meaningful discoveries.

However, the public at large is fairly ignorant of this concept and it’s fundamental importance, not just for science but also for critical thinking in general. This book aims to change that. It will use probability distributions as tools for understanding the world available to (and beneficial for) everybody. The chapters that follow will simplify complex scientific methods of dealing with uncertainty into actionable lessons we all can use to make better decisions, avoid mistakes, and improve our lives.

In other words, the book will help you apply the cutting edge scientific reasoning to everyday problems in your life where critical thinking is called for.

I am a critical thinking professor and my main expertise is philosophy. While I love math and statistics, this is not a mathematical book. It is primarily a work in (analytic) philosophy, a discipline known for prizing clarity, decomposition, and an emphasis on precise problem solving steps and solutions.

I’m also a human being (go figure) affected by randomness and it’s servants. As a child I experienced a brutal ethnic war in my home country of Bosnia, when my life took an unexpected turn. I could have never imagined that I will one day be teaching philosophy in downtown Manhattan, rubbing shoulders with students, Wall street finance guys, and survivors of 9/11 alike.

I dedicate this book to all of them. May we be better thinkers, neighbors, and citizens.

On the evening of April 14, 1865, the 16th U.S President Abraham Lincoln, walked into Ford’s Theatre in Washington, D.C.

He had made decisions under uncertainty his entire adult life. He had navigated war, political collapse, incomplete information, and irreversible consequences. He understood risk. He understood stakes. He understood that action often precedes clarity.

What he did not know—what he could not know—was how that particular evening would unfold.

From his perspective, the future contained multiple possible paths. Most were ordinary. Some were favorable. And, as we now know, one was catastrophic. No amount of intelligence, experience, or moral seriousness could collapse those possibilities into a single, certain outcome before the moment arrived.

That kind of uncertainty is extreme, but it is not unique.

As much as we’d like our world to be neat and predictable, it is far from that.

Events happen without warning. Outcomes vary even when conditions look identical. Effort does not reliably map onto reward. Patterns appear, disappear, and reappear just long enough to fool us into believing we’ve understood what’s going on.

If you are young, inexperienced, or lack understanding about how the world works, you’ll think of this as a temporary problem caused by ignorance or lack of data. But, that’s not what is happening behind the curtain of everyday life.

Chaos, expressed as variation of outcomes in life is a permanent feature of reality. The world is permeated by randomness.

I know, it’s not fair. If you put the same amount of effort into something as the next guy, you’d expect the same reward. And you’d get upset if that doesn’t happen.

Two people graduate in the same year, from similar schools, with similar grades. They apply to the same kinds of jobs. One quickly lands a well-paid position, builds momentum, and within a few years looks “successful.” The other gets rejected again and again, takes temporary work, and starts to doubt their own ability.

From the inside, this may feel like a verdict on talent, effort, character, or the society. Some people blame themselves; others, the government, corporations, the media, etc.

But if you step back, you’ll see an uncomfortable, yet profound picture appearing: small differences early on—who saw which posting, who happened to interview on a good day, who got lucky with timing—can compound into radically different outcomes.

When scientists say a process is noisy, they mean something like this:
outcomes depend not only on the things that should matter, but also on many small, uncontrollable factors that vary from case to case.

The concept of noise will play an important concept in this book, so it’s good if you familiarize youself with it right at the outset. The word “noise” is related to sound, but it adopts a wider meaning. If you’re listening to your favorite podcast and suddenly the clarity of the host’s voice scrambles under some interference (say, you stand next to some other electronic device), then such interference is called noise.

This usage comes originally from the information science, where it is understood as random effect of the unknown sources in the environment on the content of the message being transferred through some channel. What noise interferes with is called the signal. The voice on the podcast is the signal you want to hear, and noise prevents that.

Now, we can generalize this idea of noise and apply it to any other context in which information is exchanged. If you’re looking outside of your window on a foggy day and you can’t clearly see whether your favorite pizza place is open or not, then fog is noise obscuring the signal: the “Open” sign on the door of the pizzeria.

Or, if you want to take a class with some professor but their student reviews contain both stellar and not so stellar feedback, then the variability in the reviews could be considered a noise obscuring the signal: the truth about the quality of that professor.



Figure 1:Noise and signal: variability layered on top of structure.

So, noise could be understood as the existence of variablity in reality that clouds our efforts at knowing what is true. It is randomness layered on top of structure of reality.

At this point, it helps to connect a few terms that will appear throughout the book.

Randomness refers to the fact that outcomes vary even when conditions look similar.

Noise refers to how that randomness interferes with our ability to see what matters (the truth).

Uncertainty is what we experience when we have to act without knowing which outcome will occur.

These ideas overlap, and that overlap is intentional. In this book, we will discuss all three.

For you, right now, the main task is to understand and accept these three mutually related concepts as inseparable aspects of our reality. They can be further summarized like this:

Randomness exists in the world.

Noise affects what we can know about it.

Uncertainty is what remains when we have to decide anyway.

The tricky thing with them is that they are often unavoidable. There is alwas some amount of noise in any environment. It can never be fully eliminated. Randomness affects everything, and uncertainty is the default state of being.

This is not limited to careers or effort. It applies literally to everything in life.

A video posted online can receive ten views or ten million, even when the quality difference is small. A dating profile can succeed or fail depending on timing, mood, or the order in which it is seen. A startup can collapse or explode based on conditions that no one could fully predict in advance.

The numbers we often obsess over (grades, rankings, scores, follower counts, swipe-lefts or swipe-rights) suggest that we can achieve absolute precision in life.

But that’s an illusion. The processes that generate those numbers often escape precision. Randomness rules them all.

hierarchy.lvl2: The real task of critical thinking
The real task of critical thinking

records.content:
Critical thinking is often described as “thinking clearly,” “avoiding fallacies,” or “being logical.” Those descriptions are not wrong, but they miss something more fundamental.

At its core, critical thinking is the attempt to reduce uncertainty as much as reality allows. It’s job is to clear out the fog as much as it is possible so we could make decisions about what we see, and what should we do.

I want you to pay attention to this definition of critical thinking, because it points out to a few important details.

First, it is humble. It doesn’t say that uncertainty can be eliminated. It accepts that there is an irreducible amount of noise in life, and that sometimes we can’t do much about it.

Second, it doesn’t want to deny uncertainty, or pretend that it’s not there. That would be unproductive. We live in the real world and we should accept its features, no matter what they are. Reality doesn’t care about our feelings.

As critical thinkers, we neither escape from uncertainty, nor allow it to prevent us from living our life to the fullest. Instead, we treat it as a constraint, or an obstacle, to be managed intelligently.

I want to stress another important aspect of what this book will attempt to teach you. The point of reducing uncertainty is not to achieve more comfort or increase our knowledge. While those might be important on their own, that’s not what critical thinking is really about.

For me, critical thinking is about action.

Every real decision is made before uncertainty disappears. Waiting for perfect clarity usually means not acting at all, or acting too late. Acting blindly, on the other hand, means mistaking confidence for understanding.

Critical thinking occupies the space in between.

It asks: given how much uncertainty is unavoidable here, what kind of action still makes sense?

Although I am a philosophy professor (and my kind has been known to indulge in reading and knowledge collection, sometimes excessively), I don’t want to encourage you to bury your head in a library and become a brainiac. The aim of this book is not to pile your brain with yet more content.

I understand you might have different goals in life, and some of them demand that you act on something before you fully understand it. So, I want to encourage you do act as much as you can. Do things in life, make mistakes, risk. These are important.

But if you want to act smart, then this book is for you. So, continue reading.

hierarchy.lvl2: Science as a discipline of uncertainty reduction
Science as a discipline of uncertainty reduction

records.content:
Science is often misunderstood as a machine for producing certainty. But it isn’t. Any easy way to recognize a person who does not really know how science works is by seeing how they interpret scientific work and its outcomes. The fact that some people get a bad reaction to some vaccine doesn’t mean that scientists are lying to you that they work. Noise occurs everywhere, even in medical science. No scientist worth their salt will tell you anything different.

However, science is the most successful practice of uncertainty management humans have ever developed. Its power does not come from claiming absolute truth, but from learning how to ask questions in ways that make error visible, measurable, and correctable.

Crucially, science also knows its limits.

No scientific claim is perfectly certain. No measurement is noise-free. No prediction is immune to surprise.

And yet, science works, precisely because it takes uncertainty seriously.

If we want to be good critical thinkers in everyday life, we cannot ignore these lessons. We must borrow them.

You may have noticed the book’s title and wondered how uncertainty can have a ‘shape’.

What’s behind it is the understanding that not all uncertainty is the same.

For example, some uncertain situations are flat and indifferent. Others clusters around averages. Some hide danger in rare extremes. Others grows worse over time. Some of them reset and forget the past entirely.

Treating all uncertainty as if it were identical is one of the most common (and most costly) thinking errors people make.

The way you reason about:

waiting in a line,

evaluating medical risks,

interpreting success and failure,

planning a career,

reacting to news and statistics,

depends on what kind of uncertainty you are facing.

And different kinds of uncertainty require different mental tools.

What this book is (and what it is not)

records.content:
This book is not a science or a statistics textbook. You will find no formulas here; there is no math to memorize.

Instead, you should understand this textbook as a philosophical field guide through life and the myriad of uncertain situations you will face, almost on a daily basis.

Each chapter introduces a shape of uncertainty: a recurring pattern that appears in science, economics, biology, technology, and everyday life. You will meet these shapes through familiar situations, not abstract definitions. Only after your intuitive understanding is clear will we talk about it in more scientific and statistical terms.

So, the goal here is not calculation. I am not a math teacher and I will not bother you with those. My goal is for you to understand the most powerful statistical concepts scientists use in their work so you could apply them in your everyday life.

Understanding these shapes of uncertainty will help you:

avoid predictable reasoning traps,

make better decisions under imperfect information,

and stop demanding certainty where none is available.

To get the most of the content here, read it with an open mind and try to think about your life and experience as you process the concepts. Some of them might be easy to understand; others will be harder. But all of them will apply to some aspect of reality you have already experienced, or you will experience at some point in your life.

Each chapter of the book is written as a single piece of text accessible here, and shareable as a hyperlink. Throughout each of them, besides the main text, you will find many boxes highlighting, cautioning, and summarizing things.

For example, key ideas will be wrapped like this:

Key idea

This is a key idea you should pay attention to.

If there is something I want you to be cautios about, I’ll wrap it up in a pitfall box, which will look like this:

Pitfall: something to be cautious about

Watch out for those pitfalls!

Similarly, there will be plenty of definitions throughout the book. They will be highlighted like this:

Definition

Here comes a definition of a definition.

Finally, every chapter will end with an exercise. I encourage you to do them. They will look like this:

Exercise

Introduce yourself with a meme.

In the top right corner, you have a search box. It will help you find more specific content and/or take you to a section you want to revisit.

The main aim of the book is to help you gain a clearer view of the limits within which thinking and action are possible.

That clarity will change how you move through the world.

It will not tell you what will happen; but it will help you choose what to do anyway.

And, in my view, that is the beginning of real critical thinking.

Buckle up.

What you’ll learn

Why some uncertain situations are indifferent rather than complex

How to recognize randomness with no internal structure to exploit

Why repetition does not always produce learning or advantage

When persistence, strategy, and interpretation stop making sense

How to avoid reading meaning, fairness, or progress into indifferent outcomes

If you could imagine a perfectly random situation, what comes to your mind?

If you’re like me, you probably think about some game experiments or tricks, like tossing a coin or throwing a gambling die.

These are standard, textbook examples of a particular kind of randomness in which the outcome of some action is completely unpredictable.

But, what does it mean exactly to say that the outcome is unpredictable? While the answer seems simple (the face the coin lands on, or the top number shown on the die once it stops turning), it takes a bit more thought to describe this randomness in more detail.

Namely, in both of these cases we have a set of possible outcomes. In the case of the coin, only two (heads and tails), and in the case of the die, six (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6). These possible outcomes form a set and we’ll call such a set 

the range.

In probability theory and statistics, the outcome of some random situation is called a random variable and this set is called the range of the random variable. Every uncertain situation in life will have a range; you can think of it a set of all possibilities that can occur after some action takes place.

Philosophers love describing these as possible worlds and if you’re a fan of science fiction, you’ll immediately think of the multiverse.

If you do, you’ll not be far off the mark.

What makes situations like the coin toss and die throw unique is that their unpredictability is not particularly complex. Even a five year old playing a board game can understand how it works. The unpredictability here, however, stems from the fact that the result that occurs is completely indifferent towards all outcomes in the range; not of them are preferred. When you toss a die, you’re equally likely to get a 1 and a 6 (and any other number in the range). No result is nudged forward, and if the die is fair (not interfered with intentionally), there are no mysterious forces behind it.

This particular kind of randomness is called 

uniform randomness, and a set of possible outcomes together with their propensity to occur following a particular pattern is called a 

uniform distribution.

Key idea

Some uncertainty exists because nothing is pushing outcomes anywhere. We call such uncertainty uniform.

hierarchy.lvl2: The shape of the uniform distribution
The shape of the uniform distribution

records.content:
The defining feature of this type of uncertainty is that every possibility (every outcome in its range) stands on equal footing.

If you imagine this as the space of possible outcomes, it is flat. It has no hills, or valleys. Just an even spread, where every result is as plausible as the next, and none contains information about what should follow.

This does not mean outcomes cannot surprise us. They often do. But the surprise carries no lesson. Nothing about an unexpected result makes the next one more predictable, or more favorable, or more revealing.

This is randomness without internal structure to exploit.

And that absence of structure is what distinguishes uniform uncertainty from every other shape you will encounter in this book. Later chapters will introduce situations where outcomes cluster, where history matters, where rare events dominate, or where small differences grow into large ones.

Here, none of that happens.

This is the baseline distribution. The simplest case. The point of zero curvature.

Understanding this shape matters not because it is common (it isn’t) but because it will provide us a useful contrast to any other uncertain situation we’ll encounter later in the book. Once you grasp what true indifference looks like, any other structure becomes visible everywhere else.

So, before we can talk about different strategies to optimize our actions amid complex uncertainties, we have to recognize the rare situations where none of those ideas apply.

Uniform uncertainty is one of them.

And it is fitting that we talk about this type of uncertainty first, because it is as random as it can possibly get. It offers us nothing to hold on to, there are no creases on its surface we could grab, there are no details on its body to give any sense of distinction. It is pure and unadulterated randomness; chaos in the full sense of the word.

We’ll use visuals to describe these shapes in more detail, and below you will find the first one of these. What you see here is a chart showing the frequency of a die toss after 100,000 throws.

When we say that a probability distribution is flat, we mean (visually) something like this: all bars are of (roughly) equal hight, there’s nothing to indicate some numbers are more favored than others.



Figure 1:Observed frequencies from 1000 tosses of a fair die.No outcome is favored; deviations reflect random variation, not structure.
Let’s formalize the description of this type of uncertainty by looking at it’s fundamental features. We’ll answer those questions we mentioned in the last chapter.

Is there a typical outcome or set of outcomes that occur under a uniform distribution? No, this question does not even make much sense under these circumstances. Since all outcomes are equally likely, none of them is somehow ‘typical.’

In statistics, typicallity is usually expressed through the concept of the average (the arithmetic mean, to be more precise). Computing it is very simple: we get it by adding all the values in the range and dividing it by the number of the values. It is considered to be a measure of ‘central tendency’ of a distribution: it tells us what is the typical value the outcomes in the distribution have a tendency to ‘circle around.’

This allows statisticians to compute the average of any distribution, including the uniform one. So, if we take, for example, the fair die as an example and compute it’s average, we’ll get 3.5. So, in the formal sense, this would be the ‘typical’ outcome of a die toss.

But, does this make any sense? Do we ever get 3.5 when we roll a fair die? No, of course. So, this is not very useful in the immediate, practical sense. But, you can imagine a situation in which you’d want to know what could you expect in a uniformly distributed random process that repeats many times. For example, imagine you wanted to play a gambling game in which you had to pay an entrance fee of $3 for each toss of the die, and you won as many dollars as the number on the die would show (so, if it shows 1 you get $1; if it shows 6, you get $6). The game could be played indefinitely.

Should you play this game?

This is where the ‘typicality’ of the uniform distribution can help. While it is uncertain how much money you could make on each individual toss (if you get a 1, you’ll be at a loss for $2; if you get a 6, you’ll pocket $3), the average across many games suggest that it would be profitable for you to partake in the game: for each $300 you pay in entrance fees, you’d be expected to make $350, so you’d be profiting $50. This is about 16% profit, which is, if you think about it, not bad at all.

Now, this is informative. It tells us something important about the nature of this random process.

Does the uniform distribution contain any extreme outcomes? Well, it depends on how we define an extreme. In probability distributions, extremes are considered to be extremely rare outcomes, not extremely small or extremely large values.

For example, if you to a beach in Long Island, you’re not very likely to be eaten by a shark. You can spend your entire lifetime on the beach and never encounter a deadly great white shark. But, it is still possible to be so unlucky and get eaten by one. In this example (which is not an example of a uniform distribution) encountering a deadly shark is the extreme outcome because it’s so rare.

Perhaps, we could translate this to a more familiar situation: imagine a large bowl with 100,000 marbles, 999,999 of which are blue, and 1 is red. If you randomly pulled one marble out, picking the red one would be an extreme event.

Uniform distribution does not contain these kinds of extremes. You might have extremely low and extremely large values, but if all have the same probability of occurring, then they are not extremes. Here, any outcome is as extreme as any other, and there is no meaningful distinction between extreme typical values. So, the idea of an extreme is not very informative in uniform randomness.

As I’m sure you noticed already, this is a very boring type of randomness, which is also evident in the fact that it is ‘memoryless’: every new outcome resets everything, the system doesn’t ‘remember’ previous outcomes. Every time you toss a die, the probabilty of getting some number is the same; the process doesn’t care about which number you got last time.

Similary, there is no accummulation of outcomes. If you flip a coin 10 times and you got heads each of the 10 times, you’re not ‘due’ to get either tails or heads on the next flip. Those 10 heads don’t accummulate and have no impact on the future flips.

Can you successfully predict what will happen in the future? Does this distribution tell us what kinds of values we might expect?

Short term, the answer is no. You can’t know anything about the next outcome. Actually, you can’t know anything about any individual outcome, no matter how long in the future it is. Your predictive abilities are equally opaque for the outcome 2 as well as for the outcome 2,000. However, as I indicated earlier, you can know something about the aggregate (group) outcomes: you can predict the average of set of repeated outcomes.

Now that you know a bit about this shape of uncertainty, you can understand what kinds of actions are most appropriate in circumstances determined by uniform randomness. You are pretty powerless as an individual, and you’re at the mercy of the most whimsical of masters: absolute randomness with no character.

The best strategy in situations like these will depend on what is at stake for you. If you’re playing a game with some meaningful reward, but no entrance fee and no sacrifice on your part, then participating cannot harm you; you should do it by all means.

However, if the process does require some sacrifice, then your best strategy will depend on the relation between that sacrifice and the probabilities of the reward. The most common situation like this millions of people worldwide find themselves is the lottery. For a meager amount (equivalent to a couple of US dollars in most countries) people have the opportunity to buy lottery tickets that can bring them thousands, even millions of dollars as a reward. Is playing such a lottery a good idea? Is it worth spending a few dollars every month on it?

Well, that depends on how much money you have for disposal on these kinds of activities. If you do have enough to meet all your most important needs, then sure, why not. In such a context, this can even be considered a fun game, or a license to fantasize what would you do if you got a 100 million dollars. But, in my experience of playing lottery and speaking to people who do, most people don’t take this so lightly. Some of them spend significant amounts of their salary on lottery tickets, month after month, each time expecting to win precisely because they have played it for a long time and think that a mere repetition will somehow guarantee a win. But, the probability of hitting a jackpot for any kind of (large, state-sponsored) lottery is actually minuscule: most often, the odds are in the vicinity of one in a million or so.

Because the lottery is an example of a uniform randomness, each individual ticket has the same probability of outcome, the process is memoryless and doesn’t accumulate, all of which make repetitive playing a recipe for almost a certain loss. No wonder the saying that lottery is “a taxation on idiocy.”

hierarchy.lvl2: Why our minds struggle with indifference
Why our minds struggle with indifference

records.content:
If we zoom out from games of dice and lottery and focus on other real life scenarios where uniform randomness sets the rules of the game, we’ll notice our particular psychological response to it.

First, uniform randomness feels oddly clean. Once you understand its contrours, you realize that there is no sense that any effort will help, or that learning more will reveal a pattern. You can wait, retry, hope, or worry, (or try some of the gambling superstitions like blowing the dice) but none of that changes how the situation behaves.

This is, perhaps, what makes these situations psychologically uncomfortable for most of us. We are deeply inclined to believe that the world leans somewhere; that outcomes cluster, that persistence pays off, that unfairness hides a reason. But here, the world refuses to cooperate with that instinct. It offers no signal to latch onto.

The reason could be the fact that humans have evolved to recognize structure.

We are extremely good at noticing patterns, trends, gradients, and deviations. This ability is adaptive in most environments. It helps us learn, improve, and coordinate action. When the world responds to effort or feedback, pattern recognition is a strength.

But, uniform uncertainty offers none of that.

Our minds find it very hard to deal with this. When outcomes are scattered evenly, no matter what we do, our mind refuses to interpret this as absence of any structure, but as evidence of some hidden forces beneath. We assume we are missing something. We search harder, watch more closely, and if none of that gives us answers we seek (as it can’t), we reach for conspiratorial explanations.

This is the root of one of the most common errors people make, especially in gambling contexts. Go to Las Vegas, observe the casino tables and you’ll see plenty of examples like this one: roulette wheel lands on black five times in a row. Players will start crowding red, convinced that balance must assert itself. Others will double down on black, believing the streak has momentum. Neither of these interpretations are true.

You can probably feel this pull yourself. Flip a coin 10 times. If you get 9 heads and 1 tail, you’ll start being suspicious that something is wrong with the coin.

Similarly, you might feel uneasy about number 13. And you’d not be the only one. If you pay attention, you’ll notice that most buildings in the US don’t have the 13th floor.

Mystical interpretations of uniformly random events do not stop at gambling tables or beliefs about certain numbers. When people experience repeated failure or loss in domains governed by chance (such as death, illness, infertility, etc), they often search for hidden reasons: fate, punishment, destiny, imbalance, moral cause. The mind struggles to accept that something deeply meaningful can be governed by indifference.

But it can, and there’s nothing we can do about it.

Pitfall: Beware of conspiratorial thinking

Some processes are indifferent to outcomes, and if several random occurences happen, it doesn’t mean there are secret forces behind them. Uniform uncertainty often invites false meaning-making.

hierarchy.lvl2: Where Uniform Uncertainty Appears in Real Life
Where Uniform Uncertainty Appears in Real Life

records.content:
Because uniform randomness is so often introduced through games and casinos, it is easy to think of it as artificial. Something designed for entertainment, or something that exists only on tabletops and probability worksheets.

But, that would be a mistake.

Uniform uncertainty appears in real life whenever outcomes are selected from any range in an indiscriminate way, without regard to effort, intention, history, or merit. Whenever the world simply chooses, without leaning, correcting, or remembering.

These situations don’t occur that often, but wwhen they do, they cause a lot of misunderstanding.

Think of death, for example.

Not all deaths are random, of course. Many are caused by age, health, behavior, and environment. But some are not. Sometimes, death is a result of a completely random accident, lik a falling object, a sudden aneurysm, or a car accident.

When I was a middle-schooler, a classmate of mine drowned in an artificial lake, on an innocent school trip. Why did he die and not me, or someone else? There is no meaningful answer to this question.

In these cases, once the relevant conditions are met, nothing favors one person over another. The death does not become “more likely” because time has passed without it occurring. Survival yesterday does not make survival tomorrow more probable in the same way that learning improves a skill.

Each moment stands on equal footing. Each person is a candidate for such a death. It could have easily been me on that fateful school trip.

This is one reason people speak of such events in mystical terms. When a person dies unexpetedly, we say “it wasn’t his time,” or “something must have protected her,” because pure indifference is psychologically intolerable. But in these cases, there is no hidden countdown, no debt being paid off. Just a flat landscape of possibility.

A similar structure appears in many other cases in life, like medical screenings.

Imagine a rare but randomly occurring mutation or condition. If it has no early symptoms, no progression markers, and no dependence on past states, then repeated testing does not improve your odds of avoiding it; it only improves detection. Passing last year’s test does not make passing this year’s test more likely. Each screening samples the same indifferent process again.

This often leads to false reassurance (“I’ve been fine so far”) or unnecessary anxiety (“I must be due”). Both responses mistake repetition for structure.

Uniform uncertainty also governs certain bureaucratic assignments.

All of these follow uniform randomness: random IRS audits, jury duty selection, visa lotteries, housing lotteries, draft lotteries. In all of these cases, once eligibility is fixed, effort, preparation, merit, and patience are irrelevant: you can’t do anything either to get or avoid getting selected. Being overlooked last year does not increase your chances this year. Submitting early does not help. Submitting often does not help. The mechanism does not learn, reward, or correct. It is indiscriminate.

People sometimes behave as if it does. They might look for optimal timing, insider tricks, or strategic persistence. But the structure does not respond.

Even some forms of exposure in modern life have this shape.

Early-stage content distribution, like videos on early YouTube or TikTok. Random pairing on platforms, like dating apps. Initial visibility in crowded systems before any feedback loop exists. At that stage, outcomes are not yet shaped by quality, learning, or momentum. They are sampled. And being sampled yesterday tells you nothing about being sampled tomorrow.

People sometimes experience these systems as capricious or hostile. They apply expectations appropriate to structured environments. They thiink that effort should matter, improvement should help, or that persistence should pay off in a situation where none of that is pushes the needle.

Finally, uniform uncertainty shows up in some deeply personal experiences, which is why it so often attracts moral or metaphysical (religious) interpretation.

People experience infertility, sudden loss of a family member, random illness in children. In these cases, people almost always ask the wrong question: why me? But, all of these are rule by flat randomness. There are no rules who will be selected. Uniform uncertainty does not answer “why.” It answers only “which.”

And that answer has no narrative.

The crucial lesson is this:

Uniform uncertainty does not care about your effort, your patience, your virtue, or your history. When it governs a situation, interpreting outcomes as feedback is an error. Treating repetition as progress is an error. Expecting balance, fairness, or correction is an error.

Recognizing this does not make the situation easier.

But it prevents you from fighting a world that is not pushing back; because it is not pushing anywhere at all.

Exercise: Spotting Indifference

This exercise is about learning when nothing you do matters.

Identify the situation

Describe one real situation from your life (past or present) where:

The outcome mattered to you, and

You felt tempted to look for signals, patterns, or “meaning” in what was happening.

Examples (choose your own if you prefer):

waiting for medical test results

checking whether a message will arrive today

monitoring a stock, crypto price, or approval decision

waiting for news about someone’s health

anticipating the exact timing of a major event

Write 3–4 sentences. Be concrete.

Test for uniformity

Answer each question with yes/no/unsure, then justify briefly.

Does effort change probabilities?
(Does trying harder improve the odds of a particular outcome?)

Does repetition teach you anything?
(Does waiting longer, checking more often, or retrying improve insight?)

Does the past matter?
(Does what already happened affect what comes next?)

Are some outcomes “due”?
(Does the situation feel like it should correct itself?)

If you answered no to most of these, you are likely facing uniform uncertainty.

Action audit

Answer honestly:

What action did you take (or want to take)?

Did that action have any leverage over the outcome?

What would restraint have looked like?

One or two sentences is enough.

What you’ll learn

Why many real-life uncertainties collapse into binary outcomes

How meaning enters uncertainty through success/failure thresholds

Why streaks feel informative here—but often mislead

When repetition does matter, and when it still doesn’t

How binary thinking distorts judgment in life, work, and morality

Knowing how to make distinctions between two things is a fundamental human ability. Even newborns have it; fresh out of the womb, they can distinguish between everything that is their mother and that isn’t.

Because it’s so basic, it has become an integral part of how we perceive the world. Many outcomes in our life boil down to this binary choices: yes and no, pass and fail, accept and reject, and many others.

You probably recognize this in yourself. We humans are an evaluative creatures. We love giving value judgments that collapse into a binary choice. True and false, success and failure, allowed and denied. Outcomes such as these feel decisive and meaningful. They simplify our cognitive tasks and make reasoning easier.

This is particularly useful when we’re observing a process and wish to know whether something is true of the process itself, not its individual outcomes. Think about the flipping the coin. A fair coin will, on average, have a roughly equal amount of heads and tails. If you’re testing the fairness of the coin, a long streak of heads will make you raise your eyebrows and you’d naturally be suspicious.

Same goes for other binary outcomes. If the government is using lottery to choose the recipient of some welfare, if a same person receives it several times in a row, you’ll assume the entire process is not really kosher: something is happening in the background.

All of this is because streaks of singular outcomes are a signal to you that there is a certain pattern shaping the random process you’re observing.

Key idea

Binary-based processes are everywhere.

However, how many much deviation of the outcomes of such a process from a roughly equal distribution warrant this kind of judgment? If you flip the coin ten times and all ten are heads? What if seven of them are heads, and three are tails? Where should we draw the line?

Knowing more about binary types of uncertainty can help us understand this. This is important because binary uncertainty can trick us easily into believing something is happening when it’s actually not.

hierarchy.lvl2: When the world forces a choice
When the world forces a choice

records.content:
Binary outcomes do not exist in nature. Reality is complex and almost everything admits to more than two simple choices. Even the coin flip, the simplest example of binary outcomes is not actually binary. The coin is three-dimensional, and there’s nothing that physically prevents the coin from landng on the edge. If you include the rotation, there are almost infinite number of positions it could land after the flip.

But those other possibilities are so rare that we ignore them. We merely assume those other possibilities don’t exist so we could reason about it and make some predictions.

Similar things are happening when we consider other binary choices. Take passing or failing the exam. In general, when a student takes the test, he or she gets a score on some continuous scale (say percentage of correct answers) and if the test has more than just a few questions, or if it admits partial answers, then the student could get any score between 0 and 100. However, the teacher collapses the gradation of the score into a threshold: if the student has more than, say 60% or more correct answers, she passes; otherwise, she fails.

You can see that there is a lot of arbitrariness in this system. If Bob gets 59% and Anne gets 60% she passes, and he fails. The difference between them is minuscule; yet the boundary must be drawn somewhere. If Bob asks the teacher to give him a pass, and the teaches does that, then he exposes herself from another request: if Jane got 58% and fails, when she sees Bob getting a pass for 59%, she could make the same argument as Bob and pressure the teacher to lower the grade. As you can see, such an approach would be unsustainable.

All of this is to say that forcing the world to give us a binary answer is a conscious decisions by thinkers who wish to understand the world in more detail and not get bogged down by infinite-regress of adjustment. It doesn’t mean believing that the world is always very simple (we know it is not), but this simplicity sometimes needs to be forced so we could act in the world.

Pitfall: Binaries are man-made

The world itself is not binary, but continuous. We impose binary outcomes to simplify it.

Besides coin flips and college exams, these kinds of ‘collapses’ happen in many areas of life, from medicine (where some tests are reduced to pass or fail), online content moderation, instututional approvals, various admission processes, etc.

The core idea of the binary uncertainty is the reduction of some random process to only 

two outcomes. What these two outcomes are is up to humans to decide, depending on the nature of the random process.

Unlike uniform randomness, the binary one is explicitly labelled: we have specific terms for the outcomes. Where the uniform randomness could admit a near infinite (or actually infinite) number of outcomes (imagine drawing a single natural number) the binary one never has more than two.

Each of the outcomes has an associated probability of occurring. You can understand this either as a frequency (the ratio of the successes--the number of times this outcome occurred--and the total number of all possible outcomes--just two in this case), or the propensity, the tendency for some outcome to occurr more than the others.

For example, the probablility of flipping heads on a fair coin is 0.5 (or 50%). We know that because if we flip one 1,000 times, we’ll roughly get half of them heads and half tails.

Probability theory comes with certain rules that help us make the most sense out of uncertain processes. One of those rules is that the sum of probabilities of all possible outcomes in some random process (this is called ‘the outcome space’) will sum up to 1. For example, in the coin flip, we only have two outcomes, and the probabilities of heads and tails (0.5 for each) sum up to one.

Probability rule

The probabilities of all possible outcomes in some situation must sum up to 1.

If we’re tossing a fair die, then the outcome space has six possible outcomes, and since (per uniform probability distribution discussed in the last chapter) all of them are equally likely, then we get their probabilities by dividing 1 by 6: the result is 0.16, approximately.

This is useful because once we know the probability of one outcome, we can immediately know the probability of the other too. If the coin is rigged to give tails 70% of the time (if the probability of heads is 0.7), then we know that the probability of heads is 0.3 (because 1 - 0.7 = 0.3).

Binary uncertainty can be used to understand single events, such as lottery draws, or coin flips, or football game bets, as well as continuous processes consisting of the repetition of some binary events, such as shots on a basketball hoop.

When we consider a single event, we talk about something called the Bernoulli distribution, named by a famous Swiss scientist, Jacob Bernoulli. When we apply this to a continuous process, then we call it Binomial distribution (where ‘binomial’ simply means ‘two names’).

hierarchy.lvl2: How to avoid being fooled by binary uncertainty
How to avoid being fooled by binary uncertainty

records.content:
Let’s take a familiar situation. Imagine you are shooting a basketball ten times. You are not perfect, but you are decent. On average, you make about 70% of your shots.

What should you expect to happen?

Most people answer this too quickly. They say: seven shots will go in. And that sounds reasonable. But it is also misleading.

Because the question “What should I expect?” has two very different meanings.

One meaning is about long-run averages. If you repeated this experiment many times—ten shots today, ten tomorrow, ten the day after—then yes, across all those attempts, about 70% of the shots would go in.

But the other meaning is about what actually happens in one concrete run. And here, binary uncertainty behaves very differently.

In a single set of ten shots, many outcomes are possible.

You might score all ten, or none, or seven, eight, or any number in this range. And binary uncertainty helps us understand that all of these are compatible with the same underlying ability. Check this chart of a 1,000 long experiment of shooting the hoop by a player who’s probability of scoring any single shot is 70%:



Figure 1:If you had 70% chance of scoring, this show what would happen over 1,000 experiments with 10 attempts at a score in each.

Pay attention to this chart and make sure to understand what is happening. Even if a player has a certain skill level, in the repeated process of him playing the game, there will be some situations in which he will perform better, and some in which he will perform worse, than his average.

That’s simply the nature of this process. No matter one’s skill, randomness affects everything, not just in basketball games but in every other aspect of life.

This is the first place where binary uncertainty fools us: we confuse expected proportions with expected experiences. If somebody usually scores 70% of his shots, that doesn’t mean he will score (or will not score) on any particular attempt. These are averages of the process, not single events.
